title: William Orbit: Madonna and Blur producer dies aged 69
description: With Blur, Orbit produced the 1999 album 13, which saw the Britpop band take a darker and rawer lyrical turn, providing hit singles such as Tender, Co
body: With Blur, Orbit produced the 1999 album 13, which saw the Britpop band take a darker and rawer lyrical turn, providing hit singles such as Tender, Coffee & TV and No Distance Left To Run.He later worked on their track Sweet Song from 2003's Think Tank album. Orbit's collaboration with pop star Pink, Feel Good Time, from the soundtrack of 2003 film Charlie's Angels: Full Throttle, brought more success, reaching number three in the UK and bagging another Grammy nomination.His signature soundscape gave many of his recordings a dreamy, blissful aura - whether on upbeat hits by Madonna or Pink, or slower songs like Pure Shores and Black Coffee by girl group All Saints.Group member Shaznay Lewis and Orbit wrote Pure Shores for the 2000 film The Beach, starring Leonardo DiCaprio, and the track went to number one in the UK.Lewis posted a broken heart emoji in response to the news of his death.His other collaborators included Beth Orton, including co-writing her 1996 single She Cries Your Name; and U2, producing the Irish band's 2002 single Electrical Storm.Orbit released 12 studio albums as a solo artist, the best-received being 1999's Pieces in a Modern Style, which featured his interpretations of various classical pieces.The album reached number four, and a dance remix of his version of Samuel Barber's Adagio for Strings was a club smash and went to number two in the singles chart.

schema.headline: William Orbit: Madonna and Blur producer dies aged 69

title: Footballer Ivan Toney charged with assault at Soho nightclub
description: England footballer Ivan Toney has been charged with assault at a nightclub in central London.The 30-year-old, who plays for Saudi Pro League club Al-A
body: England footballer Ivan Toney has been charged with assault at a nightclub in central London.The 30-year-old, who plays for Saudi Pro League club Al-Ahli, was charged on 31 July following an incident on Wardour Street in Soho on 6 December.The former Brentford striker, who started England's 6-4 win over France in the "bronze final" of the World Cup last month, has been charged with assault causing actual bodily harm and is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on 24 September.A spokesperson for Toney said: "Ivan acknowledges the charge and although he is naturally shocked, he looks forward to being given the opportunity to clear his name in court."After starting his career at Northampton Town, the striker had permanent spells at Newcastle, Peterborough and Brentford before moving to Saudi Arabia in 2024.He was a surprise selection for England's World Cup squad but apart from the France game, his only other appearance was as a late substitute in the 2-1 semi-final defeat to Argentina.

schema.headline: Footballer Ivan Toney charged with assault at Soho nightclub

title: Streeting 'sickened' by sex abuse claims at Army college
description: AFC is the largest military training establishment for under-19s in the UK and it receives all the Army's 16-year-old recruits.North Yorkshire Police
body: AFC is the largest military training establishment for under-19s in the UK and it receives all the Army's 16-year-old recruits.North Yorkshire Police told the BBC in a response to a Freedom of Information Act request it had received 16 reports of sexual offences linked to the college in the year to June, including allegations of exposure, voyeurism and sexual assault.No information was included on whether the reports had led to prosecutions.A total of 176 complaints of inappropriate sexual behaviour at the college were made between January 2018 and June 2025, according to Ministry of Defence (MoD) data.The women, whose names have been changed to protect their identities, all attended AFC over the last five years.One woman, Tilly, told the BBC she was 17 when she was raped at AFC by several fellow soldiers who invited her into their room."They started taking my clothes off and then this led to them doing stuff I didn't consent to."And then I was raped… by multiple junior soldiers, same age as me. It went on for hours. I felt like a piece of meat."Streeting said he sympathised with the women who had been "badly failed", and praised them for speaking up."We have a duty to uphold the very highest standards in uniform and to treat every woman with the dignity and respect she deserves", he added.Earlier this week, Sarah Atherton, former MP for Wrexham, told the BBC that public confidence in the college could "only be restored through an independent inquiry".Atherton, who previously served in the Army's Intelligence Corps, led a 2021 government review into the experiences of women in the armed forces.Emma Lewell MP said: "If this was any other school or residential environment for children, it would have been closed down."

schema.headline: Streeting 'sickened' by sex abuse claims at Army college

title: Appeals court halts Trump's ballroom project paving way for Supreme Court showdown
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The White House helipad and new ballroom extension under construction in Washington DC on 5 August 2026Update
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The White House helipad and new ballroom extension under construction in Washington DC on 5 August 2026Updated 5 minutes agoThe Trump administration has been ordered to stop construction on President Donald Trump's $400m (£297m) ballroom at the White House.A federal appeals court dealt the latest setback to the controversial project on Friday, testing Trump's presidential authority and paving the way for a Supreme Court showdown on appeal."Whether or not a ⁠massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide and is not a matter for Executive self-help," the panel's ​majority said. The order upholds a preliminary ​injunction won by the National Trust for Historic Preservation, which sued after the administration tore down the ​East Wing last year to begin the project without congressional approval. Image source, Getty Images"Congress has not ceded unfettered authority to the Executive Branch to dramatically redesign, reshape, and reconstruct the White House — the People's ​House — to fit a particular President's desires," the panel said.The three-judge panel, in a 2-1 decision, said: "Each President is a temporary tenant, not the owner, of the White House and its Executive Residence.""The President has no — and claims no — constitutionally assigned authority over that property, which is designed and maintained for the use of all Presidents, current and future, and for the American people," the opinion said.The administration appealed to the court after a federal judge twice blocked above-ground construction on the ballroom, while still allowing underground work to proceed.The ruling on Friday upholds that order blocking above-ground construction without congressional approval. The appeals court delayed implementation of its ruling for 14 days to allow the Trump administration to appeal to the Supreme Court.The BBC has contacted the White House and Department of Justice for comment. Figure caption, Watch: Latest plans for White House ballroom revealedConstruction at the site where the East Wing previously stood was previously ordered to stop, but a court delayed the ruling allowing construction to continue while the appeals court considered briefs and heard arguments last month, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS. President Trump has asserted that the new ballroom is needed to "accommodate people for grand parties, State Visits", and has also said that it is "vital for National Security".He doubled down on the need for the space after an assassination attempt at the White House Correspondents' Association dinner in April.The three-judge panel on Friday said that its ruling "has nothing at all to do with whether the proposed ballroom is desirable", nor does it weigh in on whether the administration may ultimately construct the ballroom. "What it does mean is that the Defendants may not do so during the district court's expeditious litigation without securing Congress's authorization, as the Constitution and laws require," the order said.The National Trust for Historic Preservation celebrated the latest ruling, noting that no above-ground construction can take place "unless and until" Congress takes action."The White House, a global landmark that symbolizes American identity and the ideals of democracy, belongs to the American people," said Brent Leggs, President and CEO of the National Trust."The National Trust for Historic Preservation and its partners are proud to defend this irreplaceable monument on behalf of all Americans."This breaking news story is being updated and more details will be published shortly. Please refresh the page for the fullest version.You can receive Breaking News on a smartphone or tablet via the BBC News App. You can also follow @BBCBreaking on X, external to get the latest alerts.

schema.headline: Appeals court halts Trump's ballroom project paving way for Supreme Court showdown

title: Thailand shooting: Seven killed as teen opens fire at home and school near Bangkok
description: At least seven people have been killed and 23 injured after a 14-year-old boy opened fire at his home and school on the outskirts of Thailand's capita
body: At least seven people have been killed and 23 injured after a 14-year-old boy opened fire at his home and school on the outskirts of Thailand's capital, Bangkok.The gunman - a student at the Debsirin School in Nonthaburi - killed his grandparents and five teachers before taking his own life, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul told reporters. The attacker still had "more than 30 bullets left" when he turned the gun on himself, Anutin added.Nine of the injured people remain in a critical condition, authorities say.The shooting - the second at a school in Thailand this year - has renewed pressure on the government for greater action on gun control.Police were deployed to the scene during the active shooting, which began just after 10:00 local time (03:00 GMT).National police chief police Gen Kittiratt Phanphet told reporters that forensic officers had found the gunman's shots were quite accurate, with several hitting vital spots on the body.The prime minister said the attack was "well prepared" with "clear steps and clear goals".A female seventh grader, still in school uniform, told the BBC she was standing in front of her teacher when the woman was shot. "She was talking to me when [the gunman] showed up and shot her," she said."I couldn't see anything but a [cloud] of dust."Still in her uniform, with her mother by her side, she explained how the shooter stalked from room to room."I had to climb over the school fence to escape with other friends."Her mother says the girl thought she might die. "[She said] 'I thought I'd never see you again'."Another student told Reuters news agency that he had thought the sound of gunshots were firecrackers going off."There were many shots: bang bang bang. Then it went quiet. Then it started again."Students and school staff were seen fleeing from the scene, and those waiting outside the Debsirin School looked visibly distraught. Authorities warned people to stay away from the area and for those trapped in the building to hide and wait for rescuers. In a post on social media, the school later shared a call for blood donations.Other schools in the vicinity suspended classes so students could return home early.The prime minister said the tragedy "shouldn't have happened", adding "this is why the government do not allow [citizens] to possess firearms"."I don't just feel sorry for the victims but I feel sorry that this happened. How can this happen in our country," Anutin said.Thailand has strict gun laws, which punishes the illegal possession of arms with up to 10 years in jail. Enforcement of these laws has been an issue - though police have made no suggestion the weapon used in this case, owned by the shooter's grandfather, was illegally obtained.The country has one of the highest rates of civilian gun ownership in South East Asia. It is estimated that about 40% of these guns are illegal.Friday's shooting immediately triggered calls from politicians for a review of the current gun laws.Anutin responded by pledging to introduce a new firearms control law.Under the proposed new legislation, there will be restrictions on members of the public carrying such weapons."The new law will only allow government officials on duty to carry guns," Anutin said. He did not provide any specifics for the proposed legislation, including whether it would tighten gun ownership requirements.

schema.headline: Thailand shooting: Seven killed as teen opens fire at home and school near Bangkok

title: Jared Leto: Campaigners call for concerts to be cancelled
description: Warning: Contains graphic details of alleged sexual offences and misconduct, as well as strong languageWomen's safety campaigners are calling for Thir
body: Warning: Contains graphic details of alleged sexual offences and misconduct, as well as strong languageWomen's safety campaigners are calling for Thirty Seconds to Mars' upcoming concerts in the UK to be cancelled after frontman Jared Leto was accused of criminal sexual conduct.A BBC investigation published last week heard from four women who have accused the US musician and actor of behaviour which includes sexual assault and grooming. The alleged offences took place in the 2000s and 2010s when the women were teenagers and Leto was in his 30s and 40s. He is now 54.The musician - who strongly denies the claims - is currently scheduled to perform with his band at two of the UK's biggest arenas next April.The End Violence Against Women coalition and domestic abuse charity Women's Aid have told BBC Newsbeat they have concerns about the upcoming events in London and Manchester - urging organisers not to go ahead with them.BBC Newsbeat has contacted the promoters, venues and the band for comment, but has not received any responses.A spokesperson for Women's Aid told Newsbeat it is "troubling to hear that UK concerts are still planned to go ahead that will put an alleged abuser in the spotlight"."In light of the very serious allegations of criminal sexual conduct, we would urge organisers to put safety over profit and avoid platforming figures like this." Janaya Walker, interim director of the End Violence Against Women Coalition, said she backed the charity's call. "I think it really is about putting people over profit in this instance, and particularly women and girls' safety," she said.Walker said tickets still being sold for Thirty Seconds to Mars' upcoming concerts at London's The O2 and Manchester Co-Op Live was "really worrying"."Particularly for victims and survivors of violence against women and girls, they'll be seeing these reports and then seeing that things are moving forward seemingly without any consequence," she said. "I think that will cause a huge amount of alarm and frustration and anger."Walker said the coalition wants the industry to consider whether platforming groups and individuals "sends a message" about whether they "condone particular forms of behaviour"."And that's the choice that I think is in front of them."US rock band Thirty Seconds to Mars, known for hit songs including The Kill, This is War and Kings And Queens, was formed by Leto and his brother Shannon in the late 1990s.They began touring in the 2000s and progressed to headlining major arenas around the world.As part of the BBC documentary Jared Leto: Hollywood's Dark Secret, two men who worked with Leto's band for many years recall how uncomfortable staff felt about the way Leto would interact with teenage girls.One alleges that crew members were instructed to invite young girls backstage after they would join Leto on stage at gigs.Another says at one point there would typically be about two girls a day stopping by to see Leto at a house where the band was working.Among those who have accused Leto is ex-model Alex, who says her agency was invited to a Thirty Seconds to Mars' concert at London's O2 arena in 2013. She says she was later invited to an after-party by Leto's female assistant and, although she was 19 at the time, she says to protect herself she "felt the need" to pretend to be younger when she met Leto.She says she told him she was 17, and that Leto, then 41, replied: "Age is just a number, and anyway, we're in Europe."Alex says one of Leto's assistants encouraged her to go to another party at a nearby hotel later, but only Leto was in the room when she arrived.When she asked Leto if she could sleep on the chaise longue in the room, Alex says the star responded by saying that, if she did, she would wake up "with a dick in her ass".Alex says she tried to dismiss what happened, but she now believes the hotel encounter had been "all planned out".In total, 10 women have spoken to the BBC documentary, with nine of them sharing their stories publicly for the first time.Despite repeated attempts to contact Jared Leto before publication of the original story, he did not respond to the allegations put to him by the BBC.After the story was published, Leto said in a statement released by his representatives to the BBC: "I have never sexually assaulted anyone in my entire life. These claims are absolutely and categorically false".

schema.headline: Jared Leto: Campaigners call for concerts to be cancelled

title: Spain threatens retaliation if Italy fails to lift border controls over Ceuta
description: Spain has threatened to impose counter-measures on Italy if it fails to lift border controls introduced following the mass crossing of migrants into t
body: Spain has threatened to impose counter-measures on Italy if it fails to lift border controls introduced following the mass crossing of migrants into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta.Roughly 78,000 migrants from neighbouring Morocco arrived in Ceuta by sea in a matter of hours on Thursday and Friday last week.In the wake of the crossings, which saw around 100 people die, Italy partially suspended its Schengen arrangement with Spain, which included the closure of maritime and air entry points as well as the reinforcement of land border controls.On Friday, Spain called the move "unjustified" and "discriminatory against the Spanish population" and demanded it be reversed by Sunday 9 August.It added it would introduce "proportionate measures to protect the interests and dignity of its citizens" if Italy failed to reverse its decision.The statement did not specify what these reprisals would be.Italy promptly responded to Spain's warning, saying it would not accept "ultimatums or impositions" from Madrid and that it plans to keep border checks in place until at least 15 August - when it says Spain "expects a new wave of migration" to hit Ceuta.Spain has not announced an anticipated second wave of crossings. Reports have been fuelled by social media activity by Moroccan users planning another attempt, El Pais reports.The Spanish prime minister's office told the newspaper they were monitoring the situation but did not expect a repeat of scenes from last week.It remains unclear exactly why tens of thousands of migrants attempted to cross into Ceuta, but the EU's Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner has suggested criminal networks spreading disinformation were to blame - an assertion the Spanish government has agreed with.The crossings came after Spain's Supreme Court ruled that migrants stopped at sea while trying to reach Ceuta or Melilla cannot be summarily returned to Morocco.The two exclaves have long been a bone of diplomatic contention between Spain and Morocco, which does not recognise Spanish sovereignty over them.The number of people swimming to Ceuta at once has raised questions about why Morocco's border guards did not attempt to stop themThe Ceuta crossings have also caused a diplomatic rift among EU nations that share open borders as part of the Schengen area.Italy's decision to suspend its agreement was backed by Finland and Denmark, while the Czech Republic called for Spain's membership to be temporarily suspended.Morocco, for its part, has laid blame for the crisis on Spain's Supreme Court, with an unnamed government source briefing local outlets that "the deterrent element of the system collapsed and the dam gave way, not under the weight of the criminals, but of a judge's decision".Meanwhile, Moroccan media is reporting fresh online calls to co-ordinate another mass border-crossing attempt, similar to what was seen before the influx last week.Nearly 1,400 minors, some of them "very young boys and girls",  still remain in Ceuta following last week's crossings, Spanish Youth Minister Sira Rego said on Friday.She added: "There was a situation in which the system was overwhelmed, but it is now being brought under control. It is true that there are many boys and girls, and the procedure takes time."We wanted to make clear that we have prioritized the most vulnerable cases."

schema.headline: Spain threatens retaliation if Italy fails to lift border controls over Ceuta

title: Assistant referee Sian Massey‑Ellis retires to take FA role
description: Assistant referee Sian Massey‑Ellis has announced her retirement from officiating to take up a position with the Football Association.Massey‑Ellis, wh
body: Assistant referee Sian Massey‑Ellis has announced her retirement from officiating to take up a position with the Football Association.Massey‑Ellis, who officiated in more than 150 Premier League matches, will start a senior manager role focused on supporting and developing female officials.Since rising to the Premier League as an assistant referee in 2010 - becoming only the second woman to do so - Massey‑Ellis became the first Englishwoman to officiate in a men's European fixture and first woman to officiate in a men's FA Cup final, as well as being involved in five Women's FA Cup finals.After announcing her retirement, the 40-year-old said: "Although I am stepping away from the touchline, I am not stepping away from football. "If my journey has helped change perceptions, open doors or inspire even one young person to believe they belong in the game, then I will consider that one of my greatest achievements."

schema.headline: Assistant referee Sian Massey‑Ellis retires to take FA role

title: The Hundred 2026 results: Marcus Trescothick chat helped restore form - Jos Buttler
description: Jos Buttler says a conversation with England batting coach Marcus Trescothick helped him rediscover the form that took him past the all-time T20 run-s
body: Jos Buttler says a conversation with England batting coach Marcus Trescothick helped him rediscover the form that took him past the all-time T20 run-scoring record.The England wicketkeeper broke Kieron Pollard's mark of 14,803 as he recorded a 20-ball 51 for Manchester Super Giants on Wednesday - his third 50+ score in four innings.Buttler also hammered a 64-ball 131 in his most recent international outing, a T20 victory over India at Southampton last month, but struggled in the format's World Cup earlier this year, averaging 10.87 from eight matches as England went out in the semi-finals.The 35-year-old said: "Marcus Trescothick said this to me, 'if you work on your technique, it allows your mind to free up'."A lot of time when people are out of form, it's like you've got to get out your own way. You're in your head, it's mental and you've got to lose that."Ultimately, I feel like I can't see the ball very well when I'm not playing well. So I was looking at the position I get to when the ball is coming out of the hand, and I worked back."I felt like my trigger movement was twisting as opposed to staying in line. I like to get into that position where I can see the ball really well, the angle of the bat second slip or third slip as opposed to pointing at the wicketkeeper."So once I'd made the technical stuff and was comfortable and happy with that, my mindset was much better."Buttler is the second-highest run scorer in this season's Hundred with 277, behind only Sunrisers Leeds' Mitch Marsh with 290.He also has the second-most sixes with 20, again behind Australian Marsh who has 23.Former England opener Trescothick, meanwhile, will take interim charge of the Test side for the forthcoming series against Pakistan following Brendon McCullum's sacking."Sometimes, your technique can slip a little bit, in T20 cricket especially." added Buttler, who was speaking while promoting the ECB's Cricket Cities project, which provides opportunities to get active through cricket."But I think your game is always evolving and technique is always evolving a little bit. If I watch myself back now compared to when I was 25 there's differences."I do think Marcus was like right, that it was a technical change that allowed my mind to be freer."

schema.headline: The Hundred 2026 results: Marcus Trescothick chat helped restore form - Jos Buttler

title: Leipzig airport drone-bomb: Could Russia be involved?
description: A previous Russian-backed plot involving Leipzig airport could provide clues.In 2024, a parcel containing a sophisticated incendiary device caught fir
body: A previous Russian-backed plot involving Leipzig airport could provide clues.In 2024, a parcel containing a sophisticated incendiary device caught fire at the airport's DHL hub shortly before it was loaded onto a plane. Similar packages then ignited in the UK and Poland, causing extensive damage.A group of men are currently on trial in both Lithuania and Poland, where prosecutors believe they were part of a substantial network of proxies recruited by Russian military intelligence.But there was a subplot that has been little discussed before.Last September, Lithuanian prosecutors said that investigators had also seized RDX explosives meant for "other terrorist attacks". The amount was significant: equivalent to 6kg of TNT."Some of the devices were manufactured to intensify the blast," the prosecutor added.The BBC has since had access to case documents that describe how several of the men on trial were paid to transport those explosives around Europe, concealed in cans of sweetcorn and chopped tomatoes. The detonators were hidden inside headphone sets.The suspects also handled drone parts and the case talks specifically of attachments, suitable for holding a bomb.Prosecutors allege that some of the items were brought into the EU from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.Almost two dozen suspects have been charged with terror offences, but with the men's handlers still at large, believed to be in Russia, it is not clear whether the entire network was disbanded or all the hidden material found.While there is no evidence of a link to the Leipzig drone bomb, the 2024 plot certainly highlights the potential.One of the suspects charged in Poland, a Ukrainian called Vladyslav D., described in detail to investigators how he made multiple long car trips in July 2024 following instructions from someone he knew as "Warrior".He has since pleaded not guilty in court.One message sent him to the edge of a Lithuanian forest where he found a carrier bag containing "three or four packs of headphones", soggy with rain.He had already collected two cans of corn "lightly covered with soil" from another location, telling investigators he had no idea what was inside.He was ordered to leave the headphones many hours' drive away in Poland where he noticed "a guy on a bicycle" collect them from beside the road.For another assignment he received a pin for a location inside a Lithuanian cemetery and was told to dig beneath some plastic flowers. He quickly uncovered a bin bag wrapped in brown tape."Inside were drone components: small plastic propellers, I think four pieces," Vladyslav told investigators.These items were to be left by a road in central Poland for pick-up.Finally there was a trip to Germany where he was given the code to access a hostel room in Dusseldorf. He was instructed to leave the drones and other items inside.The intended targets were never revealed.In statements to investigators, Vladyslav D. said he was paid more than $2,000 (£1,487) in cryptocurrency for his efforts. His motive was clear.And what about the Leipzig case?Few details about the drone bomb are yet public.Some German sources report that the explosive was Semtex, which contains RDX - the explosive found in the food cans in a Lithuanian cemetery.We do not know how much the drone found at the airport was carrying and the physical damage may have been limited."The drone casing, if it was metal, might have put a hole in the plane but just a blast wave probably would just have dented it unless they put some fragmentation inside," explosives expert Professor Jackie Akhavan of Cranfield University explained.But if Russia was behind this, its aim was more likely to sow fear.Andrei Soldatov, an expert on Russia's intelligence agencies, said it "makes sense" to suspect Moscow, pointing to a clear pattern of sabotage and hostile activity, from arson attacks on facilities supporting Ukraine to drones over sensitive sites in Europe.Germany is one of Kyiv's biggest suppliers of military aid."It's a message. You get something like that [bomb] into one of the biggest European airports and you send the message that, 'Guys, we can do that. Remember'," Soldatov explained."You hint to the adversary that you might cause a really big problem: that tomorrow might be more serious."And the potential motive? Moscow is under intense pressure from Ukraine's long-scale drone attacks, he said, and the fact that Russian President Vladimir Putin "has been humiliated, repeatedly"."We are aware of the incident, which the German authorities continue to investigate," a Nato official told the BBC.Antonov Airlines has also been cautious so far in its response.The firm supplies planes for certain Nato operations but declined to say whether that includes military support for Ukraine.Asked whether the Ukrainian planes might have been targeted, a spokeswoman in Kyiv told the BBC: "We are not making any such assumptions…We don't know what this drone was or why it was there."But Russia watchers are clear."This is Russian interference," said John Lough of the New Eurasian Strategies (NEST) Centre. "It's all part of undermining support for Ukraine by pointing to the dangers of escalation and, frankly, scaring the German authorities."He sees high potential for a surge in such hybrid attacks now because Ukraine has "changed the balance" of the war."My expectation is that such activity will increase quite sharply over the coming months. I think it's a dangerous moment."

schema.headline: Leipzig airport drone-bomb: Could Russia be involved?

title: Guinness: 162-year-old bottle of stout found off the coast of Dover
description: Divers find 162-year-old Guinness in shipwreck off the English coastImage source, Stefan PanisImage caption, The bottle of Guinness dates back to 1864
body: Divers find 162-year-old Guinness in shipwreck off the English coastImage source, Stefan PanisImage caption, The bottle of Guinness dates back to 1864ByAdam MandevilleBBC News NIHow far would you travel for a pint of Guinness? If the answer is to the bottom of the sea, you might be in luck.There's just one catch - the pint in question is 162 years old.When Belgian underwater photographer Stefan Panis discovered a bottle buried in a shipwreck off the coast of Dover in 2025, he had no idea what he had found. He just knew something about it had caught his eye.When Panis and his friend, Eddie Huzzey, surfaced, a quick rinse revealed the familiar Guinness branding. The bottle dates back to 1864."We lifted the artefact, and then on the surface a quick rinse revealed 'Guinness'," he said.Panis, who has been diving for more than 40 years, contacted Guinness to share the discovery.So far, he has recovered just one bottle, but believes many more remain buried beneath the sand surrounding the wreck and he already has plans to recover more when conditions allow.Figure caption, Stefan Panis and his friends made the discovery off the Dover coast in 2025"Seeing the size of the case, I think it is definitely a case of 24 bottles."But there might be more cases."After the discovery, Panis' colleague Pawel Truszynski contacted a microbiologist specialising in beer at KU Leuven University in Belgium.Samples from the bottle have been sent for analysis, with researchers hoping to learn more about what the stout would have tasted like.Image source, Stefan PanisImage caption, Panis said he believes there are dozens more bottles in the shipwreck"There is always a chance that we can recover the complete DNA, and then we can do a small re-brew of the exact beer that was found in the 1860s," Panis said.If successful, researchers could recreate the taste of Guinness as it was brewed in 1864 using samples of the recovered stout.'Possibility it's still drinkable'Image source, Stefan PanisImage caption, Panis has been diving for over 40 yearsBut there may be an even more intriguing possibility."There is a possibility that it's still drinkable. The question is if the sea water has come into the bottles through the corks."If not, most likely the beer would still be drinkable."And although Panis admitted he is "not that big" of a Guinness fan, he didn't hesitate when asked whether he would try the 162-year-old stout if experts declared it safe."Of course."'I would try it even though I don't like Guinness'Image caption, Fraser Hill (left), Katie Wilkinson, and Katie White (right) said they would try 162-year-old GuinnessFor some people in Belfast, the novelty of drinking a pint that's spent more than 160 years at the bottom of the sea was reason enough to give it a go.Fraser Hill, Katie Wilkinson and Katie White all said curiosity would outweigh any hesitation if they were offered a taste of the recovered Guinness."I would try it even though I don't even like Guinness," Katie White said.Image caption, Matt McCoppin and Natalia Nowacka agreed they would try the 162-year-old stoutOthers also needed very little convincing.Matt McCoppin said he would try the stout "in a heartbeat", while Natalia Nowacka admitted she would be nervous, but still couldn't resist the opportunity."I wouldn't know what to expect, I'd be quite scared," Natalia said.Noë Vernet also said the chance to taste such a historic drink was too good to miss."For the sheer experience, I would try it," he said.Image caption, Margaret Barr said she wouldn't try the GuinnessNot everyone was tempted, however.Margaret Barr said she would much rather enjoy a pint of Guinness fresh from the tap than one recovered from the seabed."Absolutely not," she said. "I'm a big Guinness drinker, I'm just not a risk taker."Image caption, Andrew Clarke said he would try the Guinness "halfway down me"Andrew Clarke, meanwhile, said safety advice would not keep him waiting.He joked the Guinness would be "halfway down me" before experts had the chance to declare whether it was safe to drink."I don't think it would age like a fine wine, but for the sake of mankind someone needs to drink it," he said."Maybe put a few more down there and see what happens 200 years from now."A spokesperson for Diageo said: "Discoveries like this provide a fascinating window into our past and help build a deeper understanding of our heritage. "Currently, our Guinness Archive team is liaising with the divers to gather more information and evaluate the find."

schema.headline: Guinness: 162-year-old bottle of stout found off the coast of Dover

title: Argos is getting a makeover - but can it attract new shoppers?
description: ByDaniel ThomasBBC NewsDo you still shop at Argos? And if so, what do you think of it?The chain has been a fixture of the British High Street for more
body: ByDaniel ThomasBBC NewsDo you still shop at Argos? And if so, what do you think of it?The chain has been a fixture of the British High Street for more than 50 years and is still used by around half of all UK households.But it has struggled to thrive in recent years amid fierce competition from online giants like Amazon, with sales stagnating.  Its owner Sainsbury's recently announced it was selling the chain for a lot less than it paid for it just 10 years ago. But the new owners say they see "real opportunities" for growth, including opening new standalone shops. Can they succeed where Sainsbury's did not?Image caption, Enrico has fond memories of using Argos's now-discontinued print catalogue When the BBC spoke to shoppers in central London this week, the retailer seemed to divide opinion. Some, like Enrico, 28, said they loved the convenience of same-day collection, and felt nostalgic towards a brand which unlocked fond childhood memories."It was a great way of doing your Christmas shopping," he told the BBC. "We'd go into our local Argos and we'd get the massive print catalogue."Argos's encyclopedia-like catalogue was once dubbed "the laminated book of dreams", but the company stopped printing it in 2021.At one point it was Europe's most widely printed publication.Image source, Bloomberg/Getty ImagesImage caption, Many Britons have fond memories of the Argos catalogue, which the company stopped making in 2021Image source, Bloomberg/Getty ImagesFor others, though, Argos has not moved with the times and is at odds with the seemingly endless online choice. "I feel Amazon is a lot easier because it gets delivered straight to your door with Prime," said Emily, 22, adding that she only used Argos to buy appliances, not "day to day" items.Jack Cunningham, 26, from Kent often uses Argos to pick up things when he's at work in London.The scientist said the big draw was convenience: "If I need something in the moment and can't wait for delivery, normally I'll get it in Argos."You can order something really cheap on Amazon, and it might come and be the wrong size," he added.For years, commentators have asked whether Argos could build a business to take on Amazon, the biggest online seller in the UK.But while Argos has invested a lot in digital, it never quite happened. It made £4.1bn of sales last year, compared with £32bn for Amazon in the UK.'Remind people it exists'Image source, Mike Kemp/In Pictures via Getty ImagesImage caption, Argos has around 200 standalone shops, down from 845 in 2016 Argos does, however, offer something its online rivals don't - a large network of stores, concessions in Sainsbury's shops, and collection points that mean customers can click and collect on the same day, free of charge.Retail analyst Catherine Shuttleworth thinks Argos could capitalise on this, along with its reputation as a trusted British brand. However, she thinks it needs to improve its app so it can compete with online players like Amazon, Shein and Temu.  "I think if you asked people to name five High Street retailers, they wouldn't name Argos," she added. "It's almost about reminding people it exists."Figure caption, What do people want from Argos?Argos hasn't been front of mind for Georgia, 27, for ages. She thinks it is outdated and not for her. "It's very old school isn't it? I'm more of an Amazon shopper."Argos could also do better on customer service, thinks Hugh Radojev, editor of Retail Week.  "It's not an exciting place to shop, or what it used to be for kids around Christmas. Under a new ownership you'd hope they could get it back into the zeitgeist." Image caption, Nicole wants Argos to open more standalone shopsSince 2012, Argos has gone from having 845 standalone shops to around 200 - although it also has opened about 450 shop-within-shops in Sainsbury's stores. This was seen as a smart move, allowing Argos to tap into Sainsbury's large customer base. Argos will keep all of those concessions after the takeover, and customers will continue to get Nectar loyalty card points for all their purchases.But Nicole, 40, an Argos fan from South London, says she wants the chain to expand further."It would be nice if they could go in other supermarkets like Tesco," she added.'Argos has a history of being different'Argos's new owners have ruled out deals with rival supermarkets, but they do plan to forge other "partnerships" and open new standalone stores. The group, called Swift Partners, includes several seasoned retail veterans, one of them a former boss of Co-operative Group. Retail analyst Richard Hyman thinks this ownership will be a better fit than Sainsbury's, which was focused on selling food. But he is sceptical about how much Argos can grow in such a "tough retail market".Shuttleworth is more optimistic, saying with a "ruthless focus" Argos can thrive and even put Amazon under pressure."Argos completely revolutionised the way we shop when they came out and they have a history of being different," she said. "If I was marketing director I would be thinking about how to bottle that for 2027."Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.Get in touchHow will you be affected by the issues in this story? Share your experiences

schema.headline: Argos is getting a makeover - but can it attract new shoppers?

title: Gianni Infantino: Norway call for Fifa president to resign but Mexico and Argentina show support
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Norway Football Federation Lise Klaveness has long been a critic of InfantinoByAlex BrothertonBBC Sport journ
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Norway Football Federation Lise Klaveness has long been a critic of InfantinoByAlex BrothertonBBC Sport journalist and Dale JohnsonFootball issues correspondentUpdated 4 hours agoNorway have called on Fifa president Gianni Infantino to resign following his aborted attempt to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors, but Mexico and Argentina have voiced their support for the 56-year-old.Norway have gone a step further than the football associations of England, Wales, Croatia and Albania, all of whom have withdrawn support for Infantino without explicitly calling for him to resign."He [Infantino] does not have the institutional trust required to govern Fifa stably in the times we are in," Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) president Lise Klaveness said on Friday."There is no going back for Gianni Infantino. The international football cooperation is very much in trouble, and we must have a reason to get together now, and we want to ask the Fifa president to resign now."We will see which other countries eventually join in, if that becomes the strategy from the Uefa board. We are not going to ask for an extraordinary [Uefa board] meeting, we will ask him to resign in our dialogue with Fifa."Klaveness, who is a qualified lawyer, went through a list of concerns that the Norwegian FA has expressed to Fifa during her four-year tenure.Among them were questions around the awarding of tournaments, the inaugural Fifa peace prize that was awarded to US President ​Donald Trump in December, and the overturning of a ban for American forward Folarin Balogun during the recent World Cup following a phone call from Trump.Fifa has been approached for comment.Meanwhile, earlier on Friday the Mexican Football Federation broke ranks with its regional governing body Concacaf to come out in support of Infantino.Concacaf, which runs football in North and Central America and the Caribbean, called for a "comprehensive reckoning" of Infantino's presidency after he aborted plans to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.However, 2026 World Cup co-hosts Mexico have backed Infantino's leadership amid widespread calls for him to resign."The FMF [Mexican FA] supports president Infantino's leadership in continuing to promote the development of football through institutional strengthening," a statement read.It echoed a statement from Conmebol - South America's governing body - in saying it would reject any attempt to remove Infantino without a vote involving all 211 Fifa members.However, Conmebol did "express its concern about the repeated unilateral actions taken without resorting to dialogue or the institutional mechanisms provided for dealing with this type of situation".Meanwhile, the football association of 2026 World Cup runners-up Argentina praised Infantino for recognising and apologising for his "errors".It described his decade-long tenure as Fifa president as "centred on the development of soccer worldwide and institutional strength based on a clear, stable, and transparent governance model".Infantino is unanimously backed by the Confederation of African Football (CAF), but faces opposition from European football's governing Uefa and Concacaf.European teams could still boycott the World Cup as Uefa said its conditions had not been met, despite Infantino's plan being aborted.Uefa has already said it has lost confidence in Infantino, calling the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal a "shabby, back room, opaque deal".The English FA has sent a letter withdrawing its support for Infantino, while Wales, Albania and Croatia are among other individual associations to have turned their back on the 56-year-old.Concacaf described Infantino's proposal as "a symptom of leadership that has stopped putting football first", and that "this recent unilateral and egregious act of poor governance and leadership follows a pattern of missteps and similar behaviour".However, unlike Uefa, it did not go as far as to say it had lost confidence in the Fifa president. Before Infantino withdrew his proposal, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) said it stood "in solidarity" with Uefa and Concacaf in opposition to the plans. Figure caption, Why Uefa could still boycott the World CupHow the election of a Fifa president worksOrdinarily, Infantino would not be able to stand for re-election in March.The maximum tenure under Fifa statutes is three four-year terms, and Infantino is hoping to be voted in for a fourth time.However, after replacing Sepp Blatter in 2016, his first term lasted only three years. He successfully argued this one should not count, which allows him to stand again.Infantino was re-elected in 2019 and 2023 unopposed, and before the FFE controversy it looked certain the same would apply in 2027.Now Uefa and Infantino's other opponents must try to find a candidate to stand against him.The deadline for names to be put forward, together with at least five letters of support from member associations, is 18 November.The election, by secret ballot, will then take place at the 77th Fifa Congress in Rabat, Morocco on 18 March.If two candidates stand for election, a simple majority of the 211 member associations is required to win.If there are three or more candidates, 75% of votes is required to win outright. If that threshold is not met, the candidate with the fewest votes is removed and another vote is held.Once the field is reduced to two candidates, it becomes a simple majority.How likely is it that Infantino would win an election?Unless Uefa can find a way to unseat Infantino, he has seven months to cement his supporter base.One way Infantino has always done this is by jetting off around the world and meeting people.When he was elected in 2016, Infantino declared that Uefa gave him a budget of €500,000 (£430,000), external "to fund flights - mainly flights - around the world" to lobby member associations for votes.Following Wednesday's meeting of the Fifa management board in Rabat, Infantino jetted off to South America for the inauguration of new Colombian president Abelardo de la Espriella.Another key tool will be the funding of the 211 member associations, which has enabled Infantino to build loyalty around the world.This is especially true among developing nations who cannot afford to pay for football development.Crucially, the latest iteration of Infantino's investment programme, Fifa Forward 3.0, ends in December. It has given all national associations up to $8m (£5.94m) in the latest four-year cycle, a 30% increase on the last one.When announced, Fifa Forward 4.0 may well up the level of funding again.For this reason, outside of Europe, Infantino still has a great deal of support and would be the favourite to win an election.Uefa (55 members)Infantino's staunchest critics, though a few could break the block vote against him.Africa (54)The African confederation has reaffirmed its unanimous support for Infantino.   Asia (46)While the Asian confederation joined Uefa in criticising FFE it did not issue any statement after the plan was aborted. So far, only Jordan - who did not support Infantino anyway - has said it will not vote for him.Concacaf (35)Has strongly criticised Infantino, but Mexico has already broken away to back the president. With so many small nations in the region which benefit from Infantino's funding, it is unknown how much of the rest of the block will hold.Oceania (11)The OFC will not offer a statement until it holds a meeting next month, but earlier this year president Lambert Maltock called Infantino a "leader par excellence" and lauded his investment in grassroots. South America (10)A statement issued on Thursday amounted to "do it again and we won't vote for you", but Infantino can still count on Conmebol. Argentina and Paraguay are among the countries to publicly back his re-election.

schema.headline: Gianni Infantino: Norway call for Fifa president to resign but Mexico and Argentina show support

title: Premier League: Why do the world's best footballers move elsewhere?
description: Since the Premier League began in 1992, only three players have won the men's Ballon d'Or while representing an English top-flight club: Liverpool's M
body: Since the Premier League began in 1992, only three players have won the men's Ballon d'Or while representing an English top-flight club: Liverpool's Michael Owen in 2001, Manchester United's Cristiano Ronaldo in 2008 and Manchester City's Rodri in 2024.What England has been exceptionally good at is providing the environment in which elite talents become global stars.Dennis Bergkamp arrived at Arsenal after a difficult spell at Inter Milan and became one of the Premier League's most influential players. Eric Cantona had already shown flashes of his talent in France and at Leeds before becoming the emblem of Manchester United's first great Premier League side.Thierry Henry arrived in north London after an underwhelming spell at Juventus before developing into one of his generation's outstanding forwards. Ronaldo joined United as an exciting 18-year-old from Sporting, won the Ballon d'Or five years later, then signed for Real Madrid the following summer.Erling Haaland is perhaps the clearest recent example. Already one of Europe's most coveted young forwards when Manchester City signed him from Borussia Dortmund in 2022, Haaland had yet to reach the level he has in England.That is different from signing a player such as Vinicius after he has already won multiple Champions Leagues and established himself among the world's most recognisable footballers.There have been exceptions, but many of the biggest names arrived after their peak. The clearest comparison to Vinicius is Andriy Shevchenko, who joined Chelsea from AC Milan in 2006 at the age of 29. He had won the Ballon d'Or only two years earlier and finished fifth in 2005, making him one of the rare established global superstars to move to the Premier League while still close to the height of his career.Other Ballon d'Or winners such as Ruud Gullit and George Weah also joined Chelsea, but later in their careers, while Ronaldo returned to United at 36, Zlatan Ibrahimovic arrived at 34, and Jurgen Klinsmann signed for Tottenham at 30.During the 1980s and 1990s, Serie A was both enormously wealthy and the undisputed home of football's biggest stars.Diego Maradona left Barcelona for Napoli. Brazil's Ronaldo moved from Barcelona to Inter at his explosive peak. Michel Platini, Marco van Basten, Lothar Matthaus and Zinedine Zidane all spent some of the finest years of their careers in Italy.But the Premier League's financial dominance has produced a different transfer market.English clubs spend enormous sums, but it can be distributed across deep squads or on players already proven within the competition.Alexander Isak, Morgan Rogers, Elliot Anderson, Moises Caicedo, Declan Rice and Jack Grealish have all moved between Premier League clubs for more than £100m.Others, such as Liverpool's Florian Wirtz, arrive from overseas with enormous reputations but with their best years potentially still ahead.The model is less about importing one 'Galactico' and more about assembling 18-22 elite players capable of surviving a demanding season.Real Madrid and Barcelona are difficult for English clubs to compete with when the world's most coveted players become available.Jude Bellingham is a striking example. Having left Birmingham City for Borussia Dortmund to continue his development, the England midfielder moved to Real Madrid rather than back to his home country.He remains the only player to represent England's senior men's team during the Premier League era without making an appearance in the competition.Kylian Mbappe was linked with several clubs elsewhere before fulfilling his ambition of joining Real Madrid, while Neymar chose Barcelona over interest from Premier League teams when leaving Santos in 2013 - attracted in part by the chance to play alongside Lionel Messi.Cristiano Ronaldo left Manchester United for Real Madrid a year after winning the Ballon d'Or, while Luis Suarez joined Barcelona months after winning the Premier League Golden Boot and PFA Players' Player of the Year with Liverpool.And Gareth Bale and Eden Hazard swapped London for Madrid after establishing themselves among the Premier League's leading players. Bale joined Real from Tottenham in 2013 after winning the PFA Players' Player of the Year award for a second time, while Hazard made the same move from Chelsea six years later, having previously won the league's top individual honour.Harry Kane later departed Tottenham for Bayern Munich despite sitting only 47 goals behind Alan Shearer's Premier League record of 260.There are practical attractions to Spain - climate, lifestyle and, for many South American players, linguistic and cultural familiarity - but the appeal runs deeper.Real Madrid and Barcelona carry a particular status as destination clubs, reinforced by their Champions League history, global reach and association with individual honours such as the Ballon d'Or.Both have been interested in Rodri this summer.

schema.headline: Premier League: Why do the world's best footballers move elsewhere?
